ui.home.title: Your dog’s path to Japan, mapped out step by step.
ui.home.lede: Bringing a dog into Japan involves microchips, blood tests, strict deadlines, and government paperwork — in an order that matters. This tool turns all of that into a personalized checklist for your situation, built from real experience so you don’t have to learn every lesson the hard way.
ui.home.import: Already started on another device? Import your checklist →
ui.home.f1.title: Personalized, not generic
ui.home.f1.body: Answer a few plain-language questions about your dog and your country, and get a checklist tailored to your exact situation — including the simplified path if you’re coming from one of the handful of rabies-free “designated regions.”
ui.home.f2.title: The deadlines, calculated for you
ui.home.f2.body: The FAVN blood test’s 180-day wait, its 2-year outer limit, and safe booster timing all get worked out automatically from your dates — including safety buffers sized to how bad it is if you miss them.
ui.home.f3.title: A checklist you actually check off
ui.home.f3.body: Track your progress, print it, or come back later — your answers and progress are saved right on your device.
ui.home.why.title: Why this exists
ui.home.why.body: This app exists because someone went through this process for real — the confusing forms, the vet visits, the conflicting advice, the deadlines that quietly reset to zero if you get them wrong — and wanted to spare the next person some of that stress. It’s a work in progress, and it’ll keep improving as more people share what they learn.
ui.home.before.title: Before you dive in
ui.home.before.body: This tool focuses on dogs traveling to Japan from anywhere else in the world. It’s built and maintained by pet owners, not lawyers or vets — always confirm current, exact requirements with your own veterinarian, your country’s export authority, and Japan’s Animal Quarantine Service before you travel. Rules can and do change.

ui.story.title: Our story
ui.story.note: This account is accurate to our actual timeline, including real dates. We’ve left out the city, the clinic, and other people’s names — everything else here happened as described.
ui.story.started.p1: On March 24, 2026, our vet in Canada confirmed the ISO-compliant microchip our dog has had since 2014, gave his second rabies vaccination (the first was in 2024), and drew blood for the antibody test Japan requires — all in one visit. Japan allows the blood draw on the same day as the second vaccination; a dog starting from scratch couldn’t compress it this far, because the chip has to come first, then two vaccinations at least 30 days apart, and only then the blood draw. That single date became the anchor for everything downstream: a 180-day minimum wait before travel, a 2-year outer limit on the test result, and a chain of booster and retest deadlines that all trace back to it.
ui.story.started.p2: Four separate pieces had to line up correctly: the right kind of microchip, the right kind of rabies vaccine, a blood sample sent to a lab Japan actually recognizes, and a Japan-specific import form that our own country’s standard export paperwork doesn’t cover. A fifth complication sat underneath all of it — our dog has a heart condition, and a possible surgery meant the travel date itself couldn’t be treated as fixed.
ui.story.advice.h: Advice that needed a second look
ui.story.advice.p1: A vet mentioned, in passing, that our documents needed blue-ink signatures. We couldn’t find that requirement in Japan’s rules, and an original document isn’t something you casually redo, so we chased it down. Japan’s official import guide specifies no signature ink color at all — it rules out pencil, erasable ink and correction fluid, which is a different requirement — and a designated lab’s own FAQ says a black-ink signature on the antibody test report is fine. We were ready to call it a myth. Then CFIA told us in writing that it does require a wet blue-ink signature from our vet on the rabies vaccination certificates we bring to the endorsement appointment, and recommended a wet-ink signature on the original Japan health certificate. The vet was right — just about a different document, and a different authority, than we first assumed. The lesson: Japan’s rules and your own export authority’s rules are separate, so check each one directly.
ui.story.advice.p2: The same pattern showed up with the export certificate itself. Our home country issues a standard, generic international health certificate that covers exporting an animal to most destinations. Japan is not “most destinations”: it has its own recommended form, any certificate it accepts has to cover everything on that form, and our own country’s official guidance says not to use the generic certificate when the destination country supplies its own. We only caught this by reading past the first search result and cross-checking two official sources against each other — and it changed which document our vet actually needed to complete.
ui.story.country.h: The country nobody could agree on
ui.story.country.p1: The most genuinely unresolved question we ran into wasn’t about Japan at all — it was about our own route there. Our dog lives in Canada, was microchipped and vaccinated in Canada, and had blood drawn in Canada that was then shipped to a laboratory in the United States, simply because that’s where an approved lab exists. Our travel plan adds a third leg: driving from Canada into the United States, an overnight stay, then a direct flight to Japan from a U.S. airport the next day — under 24 hours on U.S. soil in total.
ui.story.country.p2: That raises a specific question: for Japan’s paperwork, which country is the exporting country — Canada, where our dog lives and where every vaccination and test actually took place, or the United States, where the international flight physically departs from? We asked this in more than one place and got two different confident answers. A Canada-focused resource treated Canada as the exporting country by default and didn’t address the U.S. leg at all. A resource focused on airline and airport requirements framed the country of departure as what matters, which points to the United States instead. Neither source was wrong on its own terms — each was answering from its own slice of the process, and neither accounted for a route that touches both countries.
ui.story.country.p3: We have not found one authoritative source that resolves this directly. The practical consequence: we are arranging export certification from both countries — a Canadian-endorsed certificate through our own official channel, and a U.S.-endorsed one as well — rather than guessing which one gets checked at the airport. That’s more paperwork and more cost than either certificate alone. Given how much a wrong guess would cost us, redundancy is the correct trade.
ui.story.deadlines.h: Deadlines that fail in two different ways
ui.story.deadlines.p1: Once the vaccination and blood test were done, the real planning started, because that test result has a shelf life, and it can expire in two different ways with two very different consequences. The result must be at least 180 days old before travel, and it stays valid for 2 years total from the draw date — but only if our dog’s rabies vaccine coverage never lapses in between. From our March 24, 2026 draw date, that gave us a window opening in late September 2026 and closing in March 2028.
ui.story.deadlines.p2: Those two limits fail differently. If our travel date ever slipped past the 2-year mark, that’s recoverable: we’d get a second blood test. We first assumed that would start a new 180-day clock, but Japan’s own import guide says otherwise — as long as rabies coverage never lapsed and the second draw is at least 180 days after the first (ours easily would be), the new result counts as soon as it’s back from the lab, with no second wait. If a rabies booster were ever given even a day after the previous one’s labeled protection period ended, the entire process resets — new vaccination series, new blood test, new 180-day wait, six-plus months undone by one missed appointment. Because the two failures cost so differently, we treat them differently: a retest only needs enough lead time for the lab result to come back, while every future booster gets closer to six weeks of margin — marked on an actual calendar, not left to memory.
ui.story.paperwork.h: Why this was never just paperwork
ui.story.paperwork.p1: Our dog’s heart condition meant a real chance of surgery interrupting our timeline. Understanding exactly how much flexibility the 180-day and 2-year rules actually allow — and confirming that a delayed trip costs us nothing as long as vaccine coverage stays unbroken — separated a medical decision from a paperwork deadline. That distinction mattered more to us than any individual form.
ui.story.sharing.p1: None of this was insurmountable. It took more research and more cross-checking than it should have, because well-meaning advice was sometimes accurate, sometimes outdated, and sometimes simply built for a route that crosses one country instead of three. We built this tool so the next person starts with a clearer map — including an honest account of the one question we still haven’t fully resolved. If you find a more definitive answer on the exporting-country question than we have, tell us: it’s the single biggest gap left in this checklist.

wizard.label: Which country are you starting from?
wizard.help: This determines whether you're on the full antibody-test path or the simplified path for a handful of rabies-free ‘designated regions.’
wizard.why: Japan treats countries very differently depending on rabies status. A short list of ‘designated regions’ (currently Iceland, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Hawaii, and Guam) get a simplified path based on residency, with no FAVN blood test required. Every other country goes through the full process: microchip, two rabies vaccinations, a FAVN antibody test, and a mandatory 180-day wait. This one answer determines which of two completely different checklists you'll see, so it's worth double-checking before moving on.

wizard.label: What's your dog's name?
wizard.help: Just so we can personalize your checklist. Totally optional.
wizard.why: Purely cosmetic — it just lets your checklist say "[Name]'s checklist" instead of "Your checklist." It has zero effect on any requirement, deadline, or document.

wizard.label: What breed is your dog?
wizard.help: Optional — helps us flag breed-specific flying considerations.
wizard.why: Also cosmetic for the checklist header, but flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds are worth naming because many airlines restrict or refuse them in cargo, and some effectively require a vet consultation before booking. This doesn't change any Japan-side paperwork requirement — that's covered by the health-conditions question next.

wizard.label: Does your dog have any of the following?
wizard.help: This is about flying safely, not about your Japan paperwork — but it can affect timing and vet sign-off, so it's worth flagging up front.
wizard.why: Japan's import rules don't care about your dog's health beyond a basic pre-export clinical exam. This question exists for your dog's safety on the flight itself: heart conditions, flat faces, senior age, and mobility issues can all affect whether cargo or cabin is safe, whether an airline will even accept the booking, and whether medication timing needs planning around a long flight. It shapes the 'fitness to fly' item on your checklist, not any government requirement.

options.label: A heart condition (e.g. a heart murmur or valve disease)
A flat-faced (brachycephalic) breed — e.g. Bulldog, Pug, Boston Terrier, Shih Tzu
A mobility issue or other chronic condition

wizard.label: Does your dog already have an ISO-compliant (15-digit) microchip?
wizard.help: Answer ‘Not sure’ if you don’t know for certain — Japan only counts rabies vaccinations given after the chip, so we’ll treat those as not-yet-started until you confirm the order with your vet.
wizard.why: This is the single most important ordering rule in the whole process: Japan only counts a rabies vaccination if it happened AFTER the ISO microchip was implanted. A vaccination given before the chip generally doesn't count, no matter how official the certificate looks — MAFF accepts it only under narrow conditions, so it usually has to be redone. That's why this comes before we ask about vaccinations: if there's no chip yet, nothing after it can have 'started' in Japan's eyes.

wizard.label: How many rabies vaccinations has your dog had since the microchip was implanted?
wizard.help: Only count vaccinations given after the microchip — vaccinations before that don't count for Japan.
wizard.why: Japan requires two rabies vaccinations (not one), given at least 30 days apart, both after the microchip. This number drives your whole downstream timeline — whether you still need a first dose, a second dose, or whether you're ready for the antibody blood test — so a precise count matters more than it might seem.

wizard.label: Date of the most recent rabies vaccination
wizard.why: This date anchors two later calculations: how soon a second dose could safely follow (if needed), and — combined with the labeled duration below — when the next booster is due before coverage lapses. A wrong date here throws off every date port.dog calculates for you downstream.

wizard.label: What's the labeled immunity duration on that vaccine (check the certificate for a ‘duration of immunity’ or similar field)?
wizard.why: Rabies vaccines are labeled for either 1 or 3 years of protection. This isn't a Japan-specific rule directly — it's about never letting coverage lapse. If a booster is given even one day after this labeled period ends, Japan no longer accepts your existing FAVN result at all, and the whole process (new vaccinations, new blood test, new 180-day wait) starts over from zero. This lets port.dog calculate a safe booster reminder date for you.

options.label: Not sure / need to check with my vet

wizard.label: Has a FAVN (rabies antibody titer) blood test already been done at a Japan-designated lab, after that vaccination?
wizard.why: The FAVN blood test measures whether the rabies vaccination actually produced enough antibodies (0.5 IU/mL or higher) — Japan won't accept the vaccination certificate alone as proof. This can only happen after both rabies doses, which is why it isn't asked until you've said you're at two or more doses. Once it's done, a mandatory 180-day clock starts — usually the single longest wait in the entire process.

wizard.label: Date of the FAVN blood draw
wizard.why: This date anchors the two biggest deadlines in the whole app: 180 days from here is the earliest your dog can legally enter Japan, and 2 years from here is the outer limit on how long this result stays valid at all. Every other computed date on your results page traces back to this one.

wizard.label: Do you have a target travel date?
wizard.why: If you already have a target date, port.dog checks it right now against your FAVN and rabies timelines and warns you immediately if it isn't actually achievable, rather than you finding out at the airport. If you don't have one yet, that check is simply skipped and you'll see earliest-possible-date guidance instead.

wizard.label: Target travel date (arrival in Japan)
wizard.why: This is checked against three separate hard deadlines: the FAVN 180-day minimum wait, the FAVN's 2-year outer validity, and the 40-day advance-notification deadline for Japan's Animal Quarantine Service. If your date conflicts with any of them, port.dog flags it clearly on your results page rather than letting you find out too late.

wizard.label: Have you already submitted advance notification to Japan's Animal Quarantine Service (AQS)?
wizard.help: This is the notification (online via NACCS, or by email) to the AQS office at your planned port of entry — separate from all your vet paperwork.
wizard.why: This determines whether we warn you about the 40-day deadline at all. If you've already filed, being past the 40-day mark isn't a problem to flag — it's already handled. If you haven't, port.dog needs to know so it can tell you clearly rather than staying quiet about something time-sensitive.

wizard.label: What date did you submit that advance notification?
wizard.why: The 40-day rule is measured from this date, not from today. If you filed before the deadline, you're fine even if today's date is past it — this is exactly what lets port.dog tell the difference between 'already handled' and 'genuinely still a problem.'

wizard.label: Will your trip include any layover, stop, or overnight stay in a country other than your home country before you arrive in Japan?
wizard.help: Even a short overland stop (e.g. driving across a border before a direct flight) counts — that country may have its own separate pet rules.
wizard.why: A layover or even a same-day overland stop in a third country can trigger that country's own, completely separate pet import or transit rules — rules that have nothing to do with Japan and aren't covered anywhere else in this checklist. It's easy to overlook because it doesn't feel like 'the trip to Japan,' but customs at that stop won't see it that way.

checklistItems.title: Implant an ISO-compliant microchip (if not already done)
checklistItems.body: Your dog needs an ISO 11784/11785-compliant 15-digit microchip, and it must be implanted BEFORE any rabies vaccination that will count toward Japan's requirements — vaccinations given before the chip generally don't count (MAFF accepts them only under narrow conditions, so ask AQS if this applies to you). The chip and the first vaccination can happen on the same visit, chip first. Note: microchips starting with the prefix ‘900 202’ are currently rejected by Japan. MAFF has also warned (December 2025) that some chips starting with ‘900’ have been found with the same number implanted in different animals, which can mean re-chipping and redoing the process — if your chip starts with 900, check with AQS early.

checklistItems.title: Confirm your microchip number is recorded on every document
checklistItems.body: The exact same 15-digit microchip number needs to appear, digit-for-digit, on every document — the vaccination certificates, any antibody test report, and the government-endorsed health certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions). Mismatches between documents are one of the most common reasons paperwork gets rejected or delayed — it's worth triple-checking this yourself rather than assuming it's automatically consistent.

checklistItems.title: Complete two rabies vaccinations, at least 30 days apart
checklistItems.body: For non-designated-region dogs, Japan requires two or more rabies vaccinations. The first must be given after the microchip is implanted, and your dog must be at least 91 days old. The second dose must be given at least 30 days after the first, and while the first dose's immunity period is still active. Use an inactivated (killed) or recombinant vaccine — live and RNA vaccines are not accepted.

checklistItems.title: Complete the second rabies vaccination
checklistItems.body: You'll need a second rabies vaccination at least 30 days after the first one, given before that first dose's immunity period lapses. Only after this second dose can the FAVN blood draw happen.

checklistItems.title: Confirm the vaccine is inactivated (killed) or recombinant — not live or RNA
checklistItems.body: Japan only accepts inactivated (killed virus) or recombinant rabies vaccines — not modified-live or RNA vaccines. The certificate must show the product name and manufacturer, so check yours or ask your vet to confirm.

checklistItems.title: Get a FAVN (or RFFIT) antibody titer test at a Japan-designated laboratory
checklistItems.body: The blood draw must happen after the second rabies vaccination (the same day is fine), after the microchip was implanted, and while the vaccination is still within its immunity period. It must be sent to a laboratory Japan specifically designates for this test — not just any vet lab. The required result is a titer of 0.5 IU/mL or higher; if it comes back lower, your dog has to be retested, and the 180-day wait runs from the passing test's blood draw. Ask your vet which designated lab they use, or check MAFF's current list.

checklistItems.title: Wait out the 180-day clock from your blood draw
checklistItems.body: You cannot bring your dog into Japan until at least 180 days have passed since the FAVN blood draw (day of the draw counts as day 0). There's no way to expedite this — a dog that arrives early is held in quarantine at the airport for the shortfall — so it's worth building your whole timeline backward from this date.

checklistItems.title: Know your FAVN's 2-year outer validity — and don't let vaccine coverage lapse
checklistItems.body: Your FAVN result is valid for 2 years from the blood draw date — but only as long as your dog's rabies vaccine coverage never lapses in the meantime. If a booster is missed and coverage lapses even briefly, the whole process resets: new vaccinations, a brand-new FAVN test, and a fresh 180-day wait from scratch. As long as each booster is given before the prior one's labeled immunity period runs out, your original FAVN stays valid for the full 2 years — and if you arrive later than that, a second antibody test covers you without another 180-day wait (see the next item).

checklistItems.title: If you'll arrive after the 2-year FAVN window, get a second antibody test — no new 180-day wait
checklistItems.body: If your arrival date will land after your first FAVN's 2-year validity ends, get a second antibody test (FAVN or RFFIT, at a designated lab) whose result covers your arrival. MAFF does NOT require another 180-day wait for it, as long as all three hold: your dog's rabies vaccination has been continuous since the first dose with no lapse; the new blood draw is at least 180 days after the first one; and the new titer is 0.5 IU/mL or higher. You then have 2 years from the new draw to arrive. Japan doesn't require retesting every 2 years if you're not travelling — only a valid result for your actual arrival. Leave a few weeks for lab results before you need them on your paperwork.

checklistItems.title: Set a booster reminder well before your vaccine's labeled expiry
checklistItems.body: Missing a booster is a 'hard' failure — it resets the entire process (new vaccination series, new FAVN, new 180-day wait: 6+ months blocked). Because the consequence is so severe, give yourself a generous buffer before the labeled immunity period ends — several weeks at minimum. Put a real calendar reminder on this; don't rely on remembering.

checklistItems.title: Implant an ISO-compliant microchip
checklistItems.body: Even on the simplified designated-region path, your dog needs an ISO 11784/11785-compliant 15-digit microchip. Chips starting with '900 202' are currently rejected, and MAFF has warned that some other chips starting with '900' have duplicate numbers — if yours starts with 900, check with AQS early.

checklistItems.title: Confirm your dog meets the residency requirement for a designated region
checklistItems.body: To use the simplified path, your dog must meet one of: continuous residence in a designated region since birth, at least 180 days of continuous residence there before export, or continuous residence since being directly imported from Japan. If your dog has traveled through non-designated countries recently, check carefully whether this breaks continuous residency.

checklistItems.title: Double-check your country's current designated-region status directly with MAFF
checklistItems.body: Japan's list of designated (simplified-path) regions is short and can change. Before you rely on the simplified process, confirm your country is still on the current official list rather than trusting this app alone.

checklistItems.title: Use Japan's recommended certificate, Form AC (or your country's Japan-specific equivalent)
checklistItems.body: Japan requires a health certificate issued or endorsed by your country's government that contains a specific list of items: your dog's ID and microchip, your (the traveler's) and the receiving contact's details in Japan, full vaccination history, the antibody test result, and a clinical exam confirmation. MAFF strongly recommends using its own form, Form AC, so nothing is missed. A generic export certificate is only acceptable if it contains every required item — usually it doesn't. A few countries have a Japan-specific certificate that replaces Form AC (for example the UK's EHC 6407 and Spain's ASE-3293); check your country's note below.

checklistItems.title: Use Japan's recommended certificate for designated regions, Form AB
checklistItems.body: Coming from a designated region, Japan's recommended health certificate is Form AB — not Form AC. Your vet completes it, and your country's government veterinary authority endorses it. It covers your dog's identification (including date of birth or age), microchip number and implant date, the residency confirmation, your country's rabies-free status for at least the past 2 years, the pre-export clinical exam, and the crate seal number if the crate is sealed. No antibody test is needed on this path.

checklistItems.title: Get your certificate endorsed by your country's official government veterinary authority
checklistItems.body: After your treating vet completes and signs the certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions), it must be endorsed by your country's official government veterinary authority (for example, CFIA in Canada, APHIS in the United States, or your national equivalent) — usually for a fee, and often needing to be booked in advance. Japan requires the original endorsed certificate (some countries' electronic certificates are also accepted).

checklistItems.title: Submit advance notification to Japan's Animal Quarantine Service — at least 40 days before arrival
checklistItems.body: This is one of the most commonly missed steps because it happens well before travel and isn't part of the vet paperwork. You (or your agent) must notify the Animal Quarantine Service office at your expected Japanese port of entry at least 40 days before your dog's arrival — online through NACCS (MAFF's preferred method), or by email if you can't use NACCS. Notifications made less than 40 days ahead are, in principle, not accepted. Do this even if your other paperwork isn't finalized yet — it's based on your planned itinerary. Dogs can only enter through certain designated airports and seaports, so check your port is one of them. Once approved, AQS sends an 'Approval of Import Inspection', which some airlines ask to see.

checklistItems.title: Book the pre-export clinical exam — within 10 days of departure
checklistItems.body: A vet (or official government vet) must examine your dog within 10 days before boarding, confirming the microchip reads correctly and there are no clinical signs of rabies (or leptospirosis, for dogs). This exam result gets recorded on Form AC, so it needs to happen close to your actual travel date, not earlier.

checklistItems.title: Get a fitness-to-fly assessment from your vet
checklistItems.body: Given what you told us about your dog's health, it's worth having an honest conversation with your vet well before booking flights — not just for paperwork, but for your dog's safety. Heart conditions (like valve disease or a murmur), flat-faced breeds, senior age, and mobility issues can all affect how well a dog tolerates a long flight, cabin vs. cargo placement, and whether an airline will even accept them. Ask specifically: is this dog fit to fly this route, and is there anything (medication timing, cabin vs. cargo, a direct routing) that would make it safer?

checklistItems.title: Check the separate pet rules for any country you'll pass through
checklistItems.body: A layover or even a brief overland stop in another country before Japan can trigger that country's own separate pet entry or transit requirements — these are not automatically covered by your Japan paperwork. Check directly with that country's relevant authority, even for a same-day or overnight stop.

checklistItems.title: Designated-region dogs: transiting a non-designated country needs a crate seal or extra certificate
checklistItems.body: Japan expects dogs from designated regions to fly or sail directly. If your dog passes through a non-designated country on the way — even just a connecting flight — you need one of two things: an official seal applied to the transport crate by your government veterinary officer before departure (its number goes on your certificate), or an additional certificate on transportation (MAFF's ANNEX form) from the quarantine or customs authorities at the transit port, or from the airline, confirming your dog stayed in its crate and had no contact with other animals. If the seal or ANNEX is missing or deficient, your dog is held in quarantine in Japan for 180 days.

checklistItems.title: Book an IATA-compliant crate and confirm your airline's pet policy
checklistItems.body: Make sure your crate meets IATA Live Animals Regulations sizing (your dog should be able to stand, turn around, and lie down naturally). Confirm with your airline: cabin vs. cargo eligibility, any breed restrictions (many airlines restrict flat-faced breeds from cargo), temperature embargo policies, and whether they require a direct/nonstop routing.

checklistItems.title: Travel with original documents, not photocopies
checklistItems.body: Bring the original government-endorsed health certificate (Form AC, or Form AB for designated regions) and, if you had one, the original antibody test report from the lab — not copies. Bring your vaccination certificates too. Keep everything together in a single folder you can access quickly at check-in and on arrival. (Japan accepts electronic certificates from a few countries, including the US, Brazil and Spain.)

checklistItems.title: Present your dog and documents at Animal Quarantine on arrival
checklistItems.body: On arrival in Japan, you'll go through the Animal Quarantine Service counter before regular customs. If your advance notification was filed correctly and your documents are complete and consistent, inspection is typically quick. If documents are missing, inconsistent, or requirements weren't met, your dog can be held in quarantine for up to 180 days — which is exactly why getting the paperwork right in advance matters so much.

checklistItems.title: Apply for Japan's own export inspection — at least 14 days before departure
checklistItems.body: Leaving Japan with your dog is its own separate process, run by the same Animal Quarantine Service (AQS) that handled your arrival — it does not happen automatically just because you're leaving. Apply for export inspection through NACCS, or by email to your local AQS office, at least 14 days before your desired inspection date, attaching your dog's veterinary certificates. The actual inspection happens within 10 days of departure, and AQS issues an English-language export certificate on the spot if everything checks out. If someone other than you brings the dog to the inspection, they'll need a Power of Attorney document from you.

checklistItems.title: Check what your home country requires to bring your dog back from Japan
checklistItems.body: This is governed entirely by your OWN country's pet import rules, not Japan's — it's a completely separate process from everything else on this checklist. The good news: most countries classify Japan as low-risk for rabies, so returning is often (not always) simpler than the outbound trip was. Confirm directly with your country's own import authority well before you travel — don't assume it mirrors the outbound process.

default.form-ac: Check with your country's national veterinary/export authority for how Form AC is submitted and whether it's paired with a generic export certificate.
default.form-ab: Check with your country's national veterinary/export authority how it endorses Japan's Form AB for dogs from designated regions.
default.gov-endorsement: Search for your country's official animal export authority (often part of the agriculture or food safety ministry) to find their Form AC endorsement process and fees.
default.return-import-home: Contact your country's own animal/agricultural import authority (often the same body that handles exports, sometimes a separate border biosecurity agency) to confirm what's required to bring your dog home from Japan — an advance import permit, a rabies titer test, or a waiting period may or may not apply depending on your country's current rules for animals arriving from Japan specifically.

CA.form-ac: In Canada, your treating vet completes Form AC directly — the CFIA's generic 'Canadian International Health Certificate' template is not a substitute and shouldn't be used instead of Form AC for Japan.
CA.gov-endorsement: In Canada, an official CFIA (Canadian Food Inspection Agency) veterinarian endorses Form AC at an in-person appointment at your local CFIA animal health office — book ahead, and pay the service fee online by credit card at least 3 days before. CFIA's generic Canadian International Health Certificate is only for destinations without their own format, so Form AC is the document to bring. CFIA has told us in writing that the supporting rabies vaccination certificates must carry a wet blue-ink signature from your vet when presented at the appointment, and recommends a wet-ink signature on the original Japan health certificate.
CA.return-import-home: CFIA sets the import policy, and Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers check compliance at the port of entry. No advance import permit, quarantine, or rabies titer test is needed for a personal pet dog returning from Japan. CFIA does require rabies certification for dogs 8 months or older, and the simplest way to meet it is the one you already have: your dog's original Canadian rabies vaccination certificate (from a licensed vet, in English or French) from preparing for Japan is proof enough, as long as that vaccine is still within its labeled duration on the day you return. Bring the original with you; CBSA checks it and does a visual health check at entry.

US.form-ac: A USDA-accredited vet fills out Japan's Form AC and submits it through APHIS's VEHCS system. APHIS confirms Form AC covers both the health certificate and the owner declaration, so no separate USDA certificate is needed (the alternative is APHIS Form 7001 plus Japan's Form A). A printed, APHIS-endorsed paper copy must travel with the dog, though Japan also accepts US certificates electronically.
US.gov-endorsement: APHIS (part of USDA) endorses Form AC digitally after your USDA-accredited vet submits it in VEHCS, and your vet can then print it. The endorsement fee is paid in VEHCS and depends on how many lab tests the certificate lists: $101 with none, $160 with 1-2 (typical for a certificate with one FAVN result), more for additional tests. Check APHIS's current fee page before you go.
US.return-import-home: The CDC — not USDA APHIS — governs dog entry into the US, under its dog-import rule: dogs must be at least 6 months old, have a microchip that can be read by a universal scanner, appear healthy, and travel with a completed online CDC Dog Import Form confirmation receipt. Because Japan is not on CDC's list of countries at high risk for dog rabies, no advance import permit, rabies vaccination certificate, titer test, or quarantine is required for a dog returning from Japan — just the Dog Import Form. Confirm current details on CDC's dog-importation site, since these federal rules have changed before.

US-HI.form-ab: Because Hawaii is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, a USDA-accredited vet completes Japan's Form AB — not Form AC — and submits it through APHIS's VEHCS system for endorsement. APHIS notes Form AB may only be used for US-origin pets traveling to Japan from Hawaii or Guam.
US-HI.gov-endorsement: Same as the US mainland: APHIS endorses the certificate digitally after your USDA-accredited vet submits it through VEHCS, for a fee paid in VEHCS (from $101 per certificate, depending on the number of lab tests listed).
US-HI.return-import-home: Hawaii runs its OWN rabies quarantine program (Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Animal Quarantine Branch — renamed from the Department of Agriculture in July 2025), separate from and on top of the federal CDC Dog Import Form. It applies to dogs arriving from Japan, which is not on Hawaii's exempt list. To qualify for Direct Airport Release or the 5-Day-Or-Less program instead of up to 120 days' quarantine, your dog needs: a working microchip implanted before the FAVN blood draw; at least two rabies vaccinations given more than 30 days apart, the most recent still valid and given at least 30 days before arrival; a passing FAVN result (0.5 IU/mL or more) from a Hawaii-approved lab, with at least 30 days passed since the lab received the sample (results are valid 36 months); and Form AQS-279, documents and fees submitted at least 10 days before arrival. If your dog lives in Hawaii, finish the vaccines and FAVN test before you leave so it can come home without quarantine. Check dab.hawaii.gov before travel.

AR.form-ac: Argentina's SENASA (Servicio Nacional de Sanidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria) issues a Certificado Veterinario Internacional (CVI), drafted by a private vet and endorsed at a SENASA office, tailored to Japan's specific entry requirements. This CVI is issued alongside Japan's own mandatory Form AC — Japan requires Form AC regardless of what certificate Argentina itself uses.
AR.gov-endorsement: In Argentina, SENASA endorses the CVI at one of its offices after your vet completes it — confirm directly with SENASA (responde@senasa.gob.ar) exactly how this pairs with Form AC for Japan specifically.
AR.return-import-home: To return to Argentina, your dog needs an International Veterinary Certificate issued, signed and stamped by Japan's veterinary authority (AQS), with Spanish as one of its languages — a real practical hurdle, so raise it with AQS early. It must reflect a vet health check within 10 days and a parasite treatment within 15 days before the certificate is issued, plus a current rabies vaccination (at least 21 days old if it's a first dose). The certificate is valid for 60 days. SENASA's published rules list no titer test or quarantine; ask responde@senasa.gob.ar if unsure.

CL.form-ac: Chile's SAG (Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero) issues a Certificado Zoosanitario de Exportación (CZE) for pets leaving Chile. SAG's destination-requirements tool doesn't summarize Japan, so confirm with SAG whether it will endorse Japan's Form AC itself or issue the CZE alongside it.
CL.gov-endorsement: In Chile, request the CZE from SAG online (mascotas.sag.gob.cl for the Metropolitan and Antofagasta regions, cerofilas.sag.gob.cl elsewhere) or at a SAG office. The fee is 0.41 UTM (plus 0.22 UTM per extra pet) and it takes about 3 business days.
CL.return-import-home: SAG handles pets entering Chile under Resolution 3.343 of 2026, which replaced the 2021 rules. No advance permit is needed; SAG checks at the border. Your dog needs an International Veterinary Certificate from Japan's veterinary authority, in Spanish plus Japanese or English, valid 10 days (extendable by up to 5), showing a microchip, the last two rabies vaccinations (a first dose must be at least 21 days before arrival), a parasite treatment 5-30 days before the certificate, and a vet exam. A dog that has lived 6+ months in a rabies-free country may be exempt from vaccination only if Chile recognizes that country's status — confirm with SAG whether that applies to Japan; keeping the vaccine current is the safe option. The current rules list no home quarantine.

CO.form-ac: In Colombia, ICA issues a Certificado de Inspección Sanitaria (CIS) for your dog's departure, and ICA's own list of extra destination requirements includes Japan. Confirm with ICA whether it will endorse Japan's Form AC itself or issue the CIS alongside it.
CO.gov-endorsement: Request the CIS through ICA's SISPAP platform; the inspection happens at ICA's office at your departure airport, using a health certificate from an ICA-registered vet dated no more than 5 days earlier. Questions: ICA's Dirección Técnica de Cuarentena (cuarentena.animal@ica.gov.co).
CO.return-import-home: To enter Colombia, no advance permit is needed. Bring an original health certificate issued or endorsed by Japan's official veterinary authority, dated no more than 10 days before arrival, showing a parasite treatment within the last 60 days and current vaccines (for dogs: rabies, distemper, hepatitis, leptospirosis, parvovirus, coronavirus, parainfluenza), with a first rabies dose at least 21 days before the flight. Dogs must be at least 15 weeks old. ICA inspects the dog at the airport and issues an inspection certificate (fee applies); quarantine only applies if something is missing.

FR.form-ac: In France, your local veterinary service (DDPP or DDETSPP, under DGAL) countersigns the export health certificate after your vet completes it — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC. Check FranceAgriMer's Exp@don database or ask your DDPP whether a France-specific certificate for Japan applies.
FR.gov-endorsement: Book an appointment with your local DDPP/DDETSPP to have the certificate countersigned by an official veterinarian.
FR.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left France on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. On arrival in France, go to customs (douane) with your dog and documents; no advance appointment is needed.

DE.form-ac: In Germany, your local Veterinäramt (district veterinary office) certifies the health certificate for travel outside the EU — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC or an equivalent certificate. Book an appointment in advance; some offices ask for several working days' notice.
DE.gov-endorsement: Your local Veterinäramt endorses the certificate for a local fee. Check its website for booking lead times.
DE.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Germany on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Present your dog to customs (Zoll) or the official veterinary service at your point of entry.

IT.form-ac: In Italy, the official veterinarian of your local ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale) issues or endorses the health certificate for travel outside the EU — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC.
IT.gov-endorsement: Contact your local ASL veterinary service well in advance to arrange the official certification.
IT.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Italy on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. On arrival, declare your dog to Italian customs (Agenzia delle Dogane), which checks the documents and microchip with veterinary border-post support if needed. Italy does not require tapeworm treatment.

ES.form-ac: For Japan, Spain issues a dedicated digital certificate, ASE-3293. Your registered (colegiado) vet requests it through MAPA's CEXGAN system, and MAPA's border veterinary inspection service (SVIF) issues it digitally. Japan accepts this digitally signed certificate from Spain as the government-endorsed document. One certificate per animal.
ES.gov-endorsement: In Spain, MAPA's SVIF issues the ASE-3293 certificate through CEXGAN after your vet submits the request — you usually don't need to visit in person.
ES.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Spain on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Enter through an authorized travellers' point of entry (PEV) and declare your dog to the Guardia Civil fiscal unit or customs staff, who check the documents and microchip.

PT.form-ac: Portugal's DGAV (Direção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária) handles pet export certificates through its online Certific@+ system; you then collect the certificate from the DGAV office it assigns. For Japan, that's Japan's Form AC or an equivalent.
PT.gov-endorsement: Apply through DGAV's Certific@+ system, then collect the endorsed certificate in person at the DGAV office indicated.
PT.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Portugal on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Portugal also requires advance notice: at least 48 hours before arrival, send DGAV's arrival-notice form and your documents to the travellers' point of entry (PEV) you'll arrive through. Lisbon's PEV is closed 00:00-06:00 and Porto's 23:00-07:00.

NL.form-ac: The Netherlands' NVWA handles pet export certification. Check NVWA's Exportassistent for a Japan certificate; if none is listed, email dpp@nvwa.nl. Legalisation is by appointment at NVWA's Utrecht office.
NL.gov-endorsement: Book NVWA's legalisation appointment at least 14 working days ahead; a fee applies.
NL.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left the Netherlands on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. On arrival, report with your dog to Dutch customs ('goods to declare'); no advance notice is needed. No tapeworm treatment is needed for the Netherlands.

BE.form-ac: Belgium's FASFC (Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain) certifies pet export certificates through its Local Control Units (LCUs) — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC.
BE.gov-endorsement: Contact the FASFC Local Control Unit for your area and send it Japan's requirements in advance, not at the appointment.
BE.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Belgium on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. On arrival at a Belgian travellers' point of entry, present your dog and documents to customs right away.

CH.form-ac: In Switzerland, your cantonal veterinary service is the government authority that certifies documents for pets leaving the country — for Japan, it endorses Japan's Form AC after your vet completes it.
CH.gov-endorsement: Contact your cantonal veterinary service to arrange the endorsement; procedures and fees vary by canton.
CH.return-import-home: Switzerland applies the same pet-travel rules as the EU (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131), and the FSVO (BLV/OSAV) lists Japan as a low-rabies-risk country, so no titer test and no FSVO import permit are needed. Your dog needs a microchip, a valid rabies vaccination, and either its valid Swiss/EU pet passport (if vaccinated before leaving) or an official health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service. Fly into Basel, Geneva or Zurich and use the red customs channel.

AT.form-ac: In Austria, the official veterinarian of your district authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) or city authority (Magistrat) certifies documents for pets leaving the EU — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC.
AT.gov-endorsement: Contact your district or city official veterinarian to arrange the endorsement. If needed, the federal consumer-health office (BAVG) can authenticate the official vet's signature.
AT.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Austria on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. In Austria, customs does the check: use the red 'goods to declare' channel.

AU.form-ab: Australia is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, so Japan's Form AB applies, not Form AC. Your vet fills in Form AB, then DAFF (Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry) endorses it or issues an equivalent official certificate, after you lodge a Notice of Intention (NOI) to Export Live Animals and the pre-export inspection is done.
AU.gov-endorsement: In Australia, lodge DAFF's Notice of Intention (NOI) to Export Live Animals at least 10 working days before departure. A departmental vet issues the export permit and health certificate; NOI, certificate and permit fees apply.
AU.return-import-home: Get a DAFF import permit through BICON before the dog leaves Japan, and allow plenty of time. Japan is a Group 2 (rabies-free) country, so no rabies titer test is needed, but your dog must spend at least 10 days in post-entry quarantine at DAFF's Mickleham facility near Melbourne (permit and quarantine fees apply — check DAFF's current fee schedule). Japan's animal quarantine service must verify the dog's identity, and the dog becomes eligible 180 days after that check — unless it is an Australian dog returning directly from Japan, the same country it was exported to. A government-approved vet must do the final exam within 5 days of export.

NZ.form-ab: New Zealand is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, so Japan's Form AB applies, not Form AC. An MPI official veterinarian endorses it or issues MPI's official export certificate under MPI's 'Dogs and Cats to Japan' requirements; an Animal Welfare Export Certificate is usually also required.
NZ.gov-endorsement: In New Zealand, MPI (Ministry for Primary Industries) endorses export paperwork through an MPI official veterinarian.
NZ.return-import-home: Japan is a Category 2 (rabies-free) country under MPI's Import Health Standard for Cats and Dogs (a new version took effect on 1 July 2026), so no rabies titer test is needed if the dog has lived in Japan for at least 6 months, since birth, or since being exported directly from New Zealand. An official vet must do a pre-export identification check at least 6 months before travel, and Japan's authority must send that form straight to MPI. Book an MPI-approved quarantine facility first, then apply for the MPI import permit at least 30 working days ahead. The dog must spend at least 10 days in quarantine on arrival.

FJ.form-ab: Fiji is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, so Japan's Form AB applies, not Form AC. Email BAF (Biosecurity Authority of Fiji) to book the final inspection and submit your vet's completed paperwork at least 7 days ahead; the BAF veterinarian then endorses Form AB or issues BAF's export health certificate.
FJ.gov-endorsement: In Fiji, BAF's veterinarian does the final pre-export inspection and certifies the paperwork; documents are due 7 days before.
FJ.return-import-home: Important asymmetry: although Fiji is one of Japan's designated (simplified) regions for the OUTBOUND leg, BAF places Japan in its stricter 'Group B' for the RETURN leg. A dog returning to Fiji from Japan needs a BAF import permit before it leaves Japan, an ISO microchip, rabies vaccination at least 30 days before export, a rabies antibody test (RNATT/FAVN, at least 0.5 IU/mL) taken 180-365 days before export, and at least 30 days of post-entry quarantine at BAF's station in Koronivia, Nausori (book 6-8 weeks ahead; home quarantine isn't allowed). BAF has narrowed this test window for some origins in 2026, so confirm the current window with BAF.

MX.form-ac: Mexico's SENASICA (part of SADER, the agriculture ministry) issues a free Certificado Zoosanitario para Exportación (CZE) for pets leaving Mexico. How SENASICA pairs the CZE with Japan's Form AC isn't spelled out on its public pages — ask SENASICA to endorse Form AC itself, or confirm what it will issue for Japan, before your vet appointment.
MX.gov-endorsement: In Mexico, SENASICA issues the free CZE at its authorized offices (about 3 business days), based on a private vet's health certificate no older than 5 days and proof of rabies vaccination. On travel day, SENASICA staff at your departure point examine the dog and add the final stamp and signature.
MX.return-import-home: To enter Mexico from Japan, your dog needs a health certificate from a vet (an official vet, or a private vet on letterhead) issued no more than 15 days before arrival, showing the rabies vaccination date and validity, internal and external deworming within the last 6 months, and that the dog is clinically healthy. SENASICA inspects the dog at the airport and issues an import certificate. SENASICA's published rules list no import permit, titer test, or quarantine.

BR.form-ac: Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAPA) issues a Certificado Veterinário Internacional (CVI) for Japan, requested online on gov.br by your private vet and signed digitally by MAPA's official vet. Confirm with MAPA (cvi.vigiagro@agricultura.gov.br) how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
BR.gov-endorsement: In Brazil, a registered private vet requests the Japan CVI online on gov.br (only vets can file for Japan), between 9 and 3 days before departure, using MAPA's AS-4 Japan health certificate model. MAPA signs it digitally and your vet prints, stamps and signs it. Since April 2023 there's no separate VIGIAGRO stamp at the airport.
BR.return-import-home: To return to Brazil from Japan, your dog needs an International Veterinary Certificate on Brazil's official model (mandatory since September 2025) issued by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service, showing a valid rabies vaccination, a clinical exam within 10 days and a parasite treatment within 15 days before issue. VIGIAGRO checks it on arrival; MAPA's page lists no import permit, titer test, or quarantine. Japan is not on the list of countries where Brazil's own outbound CVI covers your return, so you need a new certificate from Japan.

GU.form-ab: Guam is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, so a USDA-accredited vet completes Japan's Form AB — not Form AC — and submits it through APHIS's VEHCS system for APHIS endorsement.
GU.gov-endorsement: Same as the US mainland: APHIS endorses the certificate digitally after your USDA-accredited vet submits it through VEHCS, for a fee paid in VEHCS (from $101 per certificate, depending on the number of lab tests listed).
GU.return-import-home: Guam's Department of Agriculture requires an entry permit for every animal ($60 per pet plus a $5 license), applied for before travel. Japan is on Guam's quarantine-exempt list: a dog that has lived in Japan for at least 120 days and flies directly to Guam normally needs no commercial quarantine, but still needs the entry permit, a government-issued certificate showing it stayed in Japan for the previous 4 months, and current rabies and core vaccinations. Arrange arrival clearance with Guam Customs and Quarantine (fee applies), and complete the federal CDC Dog Import Form. Guam's published guide dates from 2020, so confirm with doag.guam.gov before travel.

GB.form-ac: The UK has its own Japan-specific export health certificate, EHC 6407 ('Export cats and dogs to Japan'). APHA's guidance says it replaces Japan's Form AC, so don't fill in Form AC as well. An Official Veterinarian (OV) signs it. Note: Biobest Laboratories was removed from Japan's list of designated labs, so make sure your rabies antibody test is done at a lab Japan currently accepts (anyone with a Biobest certificate issued between 27 November 2024 and 25 June 2025 should contact Japan's Animal Quarantine Service).
GB.gov-endorsement: In England, Scotland and Wales, you or your OV apply for EHC 6407 through APHA's online export health certificate service; in Northern Ireland, through DAERA. The OV's signature and stamp is the official government certification Japan requires — there's no separate endorsement step.
GB.return-import-home: Japan is a 'listed' country under Great Britain's pet travel rules, so a dog returning from Japan does not need a rabies antibody titer test or quarantine. It needs an ISO microchip, rabies vaccination, a Great Britain pet health certificate issued by an official vet in Japan within 10 days of travel, and tapeworm treatment 24 hours to 5 days before arrival, entering via an approved route.

IE.form-ac: Ireland's DAFM (Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine) certifies pet exports through its Regional Veterinary Offices. Your private vet completes the certificate Japan requires (Form AC), and your local Regional Veterinary Office adds the government stamp and signature.
IE.gov-endorsement: Contact your local DAFM Regional Veterinary Office at least 2 months before travel, or DAFM may not be able to certify in time. General queries: livetrade@agriculture.gov.ie.
IE.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Ireland on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Ireland also requires tapeworm treatment (praziquantel) given by a vet 24-120 hours before arrival and recorded on the documents — without it your dog may be refused entry or quarantined. Book a compliance check through DAFM's Advance Notice Portal before travel (a fee applies) and arrive at Dublin, Cork, Shannon, Ringaskiddy or Rosslare.

NO.form-ac: Norway's Mattilsynet (Norwegian Food Safety Authority) is the competent authority, but it publishes no specific guidance on endorsing a certificate for a pet going to Japan — confirm with Mattilsynet before your vet appointment.
NO.gov-endorsement: Contact Mattilsynet to confirm how Japan's Form AC gets officially endorsed.
NO.return-import-home: Norway still applies the older EU/EEA rules (Regulation (EU) No 577/2013) until further notice — Mattilsynet has said the new EU rules may apply in Norway from autumn 2026 at the earliest, so check its site before travel. Japan is a listed low-risk country, so a dog returning from Japan does not need a rabies titer test. It needs a microchip, rabies vaccination, either your Norwegian pet passport (if vaccinated before leaving) or an EU-format health certificate from an official vet, and tapeworm treatment 24-120 hours before arrival. Enter only via Oslo Airport or Storskog; Mattilsynet recommends notifying the border at least 48 hours ahead.

IS.form-ab: Because Iceland is one of Japan's designated (rabies-free) regions, Japan's recommended certificate is Form AB, not Form AC. Your vet completes it and MAST (Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority) endorses it. MAST has no separate Iceland certificate for Japan and points exporters to Japan's Animal Quarantine Service.
IS.gov-endorsement: In Iceland, MAST is the government veterinary authority that endorses your paperwork for Japan.
IS.return-import-home: Iceland is very strict. Even though MAST lists Japan as a Category 1 (rabies-free) country, your dog needs a MAST import permit (fee ISK 39,633; apply at least 30 days ahead), at least 6 months in Category 1 countries before arrival, MAST certificate D1 completed by a vet in Japan and sent to MAST 5-10 days before arrival, a rabies titer of at least 0.5 IU/mL drawn at least 30 days after vaccination, leptospirosis and other core vaccinations, Brucella canis (and, for intact dogs, Leishmania) blood tests, Angiostrongylus testing or preventive treatment plus parasite treatments, arrival at Keflavík Airport, and at least 14 days in quarantine at an approved station (Reykjanesbær or Mósel).

TH.form-ac: Thailand's Department of Livestock Development (DLD), via its Animal Quarantine Station at the departure international airport, issues a bilingual (Thai/English) export health certificate confirming microchip ID and rabies vaccination history — this accompanies Japan's Form AC, and the FAVN blood sample is drawn under DLD/accredited-vet supervision.
TH.gov-endorsement: In Thailand, DLD's Animal Quarantine Station at your departure airport issues and endorses the export certificate — confirm with them how it pairs with Form AC.
TH.return-import-home: A dog returning to Thailand needs an import permit from the DLD Animal Quarantine Station at your arrival airport: email Form R.1/1 and supporting documents at least 7 working days ahead. You'll also need a microchip, an English vaccination record including rabies, and a health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service. Dogs with valid paperwork and no signs of illness are normally cleared at the airport without quarantine, though officers may detain an animal at their discretion.

VN.form-ac: Vietnam's Department of Livestock Production and Animal Health (Cục Chăn nuôi và Thú y, Ministry of Agriculture and Environment — formerly the Department of Animal Health), through its Regional Animal Health Sub-Department (Chi cục Thú y vùng), issues the export veterinary health certificate after inspecting your dog and checking its microchip and rabies vaccination. Confirm with them how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
VN.gov-endorsement: In Vietnam, your Regional Animal Health Sub-Department (under the Department of Livestock Production and Animal Health) issues and endorses the export certificate.
VN.return-import-home: A dog returning to Vietnam from Japan needs a valid rabies vaccination certificate, microchip ID, and a health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service, and must be registered for quarantine with the border animal quarantine office. Whether advance registration or a permit is needed couldn't be confirmed from an official source — check with the Regional Animal Health Sub-Department before travel.

ID.form-ac: Indonesia's Badan Karantina Indonesia (Barantin) issues the Animal Health Certificate after a quarantine inspection; apply through PTK Online (ptk.karantinaindonesia.go.id) and pay by e-billing. Confirm with Barantin how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
ID.gov-endorsement: In Indonesia, Barantin's quarantine office issues the export certificate after inspection, via PTK Online.
ID.return-import-home: Before you fly, submit a prior notice to Barantin online (notice.karantinaindonesia.go.id). Your dog needs a health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service, its vaccination record, a rabies antibody (titer) test result, and a microchip. Barantin officers inspect the dog on arrival and issue a quarantine release certificate if it's healthy. Rules vary by island — Bali restricts the entry of dogs because rabies is present there — so check with Barantin for your specific arrival airport before travel.

PL.form-ac: In Poland, your district veterinary officer (Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii) issues the certificate on the destination country's own form — for Japan, that's Form AC — based on a vet exam done within the previous 48 hours. Bring the form with a sworn Polish translation, since district offices may require one.
PL.gov-endorsement: Contact your district veterinary officer (Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii) in advance; the certificate is valid for 15 days from issue.
PL.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Poland on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip.

CZ.form-ac: In the Czech Republic, an official vet at your Regional Veterinary Administration (KVS, part of the SVS) stamps and signs Japan's Form AC once your vet has completed it. The pet doesn't need to attend, but they may ask for an official Czech translation.
CZ.gov-endorsement: Submit the documents to your Regional Veterinary Administration (KVS). The fee is CZK 200 for one animal (CZK 500 for more than one).
CZ.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left the Czech Republic on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip.

GR.form-ac: In Greece, your regional unit's Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary (ΔΑΟΚ), under the Ministry of Rural Development and Food, handles official certification of pet export documents — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC. The Ministry has published a document on pet-movement requirements for Japan (linked from pet.gov.gr).
GR.gov-endorsement: Contact your regional unit's ΔΑΟΚ veterinary directorate to arrange endorsement. The exact pet-specific process and fee couldn't be confirmed from an official source, so ask them directly.
GR.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Greece on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip.

TR.form-ac: In Turkey, an official vet at your provincial or district Tarım ve Orman Müdürlüğü (Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry directorate) issues the export health certificate no earlier than 48 hours before departure, using a model matched to the destination country — for Japan, that's Japan's Form AC or equivalent content. Etlik VKMAEM in Ankara is on Japan's list of designated labs for the rabies antibody test.
TR.gov-endorsement: Contact your provincial or district agriculture and forestry directorate to book the official vet; the certificate can't be issued earlier than 48 hours before departure.
TR.return-import-home: Turkey requires a rabies antibody titer test from every country, including Japan: at least 0.5 IU/mL from an EU-approved lab, sampled at least 30 days after rabies vaccination. Entry is normally allowed only 3 months after the blood sample, but a dog that leaves Turkey with a valid titer report already in hand skips that 3-month wait on return. Bring the pet passport, the original titer report, and an official veterinary health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service. Each passenger can bring at most 2 pets.

RU.form-ac: In Russia, your local state veterinary station (СББЖ) issues Veterinary Certificate Form No. 1 in the Mercury system no earlier than 5 days before departure; Rosselkhoznadzor then issues the export certificate (Form 5a or a destination-specific certificate) at the border, or in advance. For Japan, the rabies antibody test must be done only at the FGBU VGNKI clinical-diagnostic centre; since December 2025 its reports are electronic with a QR code.
RU.gov-endorsement: In Russia, Rosselkhoznadzor (Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance) issues the export certificate, working from the Form No. 1 issued by your local veterinary station.
RU.return-import-home: Dogs returning to Russia (up to 2 per owner) need an international veterinary passport showing a clinical exam by a competent authority within 14 days and current vaccinations (including rabies, distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus, adenovirus and leptospirosis). More than 2 animals, unaccompanied animals, or unvaccinated puppies under 3 months need Veterinary Certificate Form No. 15. Enter only through a checkpoint with veterinary control. If you return within 90 days of the Form 5a certificate issued when you left, that certificate alone covers re-entry.

UA.form-ac: In Ukraine, a state vet issues certificate Form F-1, and a border state veterinary inspector of Держпродспоживслужба (State Service on Food Safety and Consumer Protection) then issues the international certificate based on it. Note that Japan's list of designated labs has no Ukrainian lab, so the rabies antibody test for Japan must be done at a Japan-designated lab abroad.
UA.gov-endorsement: In Ukraine, the State Service on Food Safety and Consumer Protection (state vets and border veterinary inspectors) is the relevant authority.
UA.return-import-home: Re-entry requires an ISO microchip, an international veterinary passport recording the rabies vaccination and a rabies antibody test result, and a health certificate issued after a vet exam, presented at a border veterinary control point. Contact the State Service's regional border offices to confirm current details, and be aware that wartime border conditions may add practical complications.

AE.form-ac: The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) issues the export veterinary health certificate after an inspection. Confirm with MOCCAE whether it will endorse Japan's Form AC itself or issue its certificate alongside it.
AE.gov-endorsement: Apply online via MOCCAE. The certificate is valid 30 days; the fee is AED 100 for up to 2 pets travelling for personal purposes.
AE.return-import-home: Japan is on the UAE's low-risk rabies list, so no titer test is needed. Before travel, get a MOCCAE import permit online (AED 200 per pet, valid 90 days); a release fee of AED 500 per dog is paid on arrival. Bring an official health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service plus microchip and vaccination records. If your dog lives in the UAE, get a MOCCAE health certificate before you leave and keep its rabies vaccination valid until you return; otherwise first-import rules apply.

SA.form-ac: Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture (MEWA) offers a pet export permit service, now on its Naama platform (naama.sa). Confirm with MEWA how its export certificate pairs with Japan's Form AC.
SA.gov-endorsement: In Saudi Arabia, apply for MEWA's pet export permit on the Naama platform (naama.sa).
SA.return-import-home: Apply for a MEWA dog import permit on the Naama platform (naama.sa) at least 15 days before shipment; the permit is valid 30 days and the importer must be 21 or older. The dog needs a microchip, a valid rabies vaccination, and an official health certificate, and its registration is checked through Absher. Some breeds are banned, including Pit Bull types, Rottweiler, Boxer, Mastiffs, Japanese Tosa, Bulldog and Presa Canario. Whether a titer test or quarantine applies to dogs from Japan couldn't be confirmed from an official source — confirm with MEWA.

IL.form-ac: Israel's Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (Veterinary Services and Animal Health) is the authority for pet export certificates. Its official pages couldn't be reached in our research, so confirm directly with Veterinary Services how it endorses Japan's Form AC.
IL.gov-endorsement: In Israel, the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security's Veterinary Services is the relevant authority — confirm which unit handles pet export certificates.
IL.return-import-home: A dog returning to Israel from Japan will need at least microchip ID, valid rabies vaccination, and an official health certificate. Israel's personal-pet rules allow up to 2 pets on the same flight as the owner. Whether Japan is exempt from Israel's rabies titer test couldn't be confirmed from an official source — confirm with the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security's Veterinary Services before travel.

ZA.form-ac: In South Africa, a state veterinarian under the Department of Agriculture (Directorate: Animal Health) must inspect and endorse the export certificate — for Japan, Japan's Form AC or equivalent. (The department was formerly DALRRD; it was split in April 2025.) ARC-Onderstepoort is on Japan's list of designated labs for the rabies antibody test.
ZA.gov-endorsement: Contact your local state veterinarian (Department of Agriculture, Directorate: Animal Health) to arrange inspection and endorsement.
ZA.return-import-home: South Africa requires a veterinary import permit even for South African dogs returning home — the Department of Agriculture advises getting it before the dog leaves South Africa, and to apply at least 4 weeks ahead. There are separate application forms for dogs subject to quarantine and not subject to quarantine, and quarantine (if required) is at Kempton Park or Cape Town. Which category applies to dogs from Japan couldn't be confirmed from an official source — confirm with the Department of Agriculture's Directorate: Animal Health.

IN.form-ac: India's AQCS (Animal Quarantine and Certification Services, Dept. of Animal Husbandry and Dairying) issues the export certificate/NOC (processing fee Rs 500) at a regional station (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad). The health certificate itself comes from a local registered vet; the AQCS certificate is valid 10 days. Confirm with your AQCS station how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
IN.gov-endorsement: Book an appointment with your regional AQCS station and bring your dog, a health certificate from a local registered vet, and microchip and vaccination records about 7 days before departure.
IN.return-import-home: At least 7 working days before travel, apply through India's ATITHI 2.0 portal for an Advance NOC, submitting the veterinary health certificate, vaccination/microchip records, travel documents, and (for re-import) your earlier AQCS export certificate. On arrival, AQCS staff examine the dog and issue a Final NOC (a processing fee applies); a 15-day quarantine at an AQCS station applies only if the dog fails the exam or shows clinical signs of illness.
