CN.form-ac: China's customs authority (GACC) issues an Animal Health Certificate (动物卫生证书) for pets leaving China through your local customs office: book about 7-10 days before departure; it's issued within 3 working days after document review and inspection. Confirm with your local customs office how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
CN.gov-endorsement: In China, your local customs office (under GACC) inspects your dog and issues the export certificate.
CN.return-import-home: Japan is on China's list of designated (rabies-free) countries. A returning dog (limit one per person) needs an official health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service, a rabies vaccination certificate, a microchip, and a clinical exam within 14 days before arrival. If everything checks out at the port, the dog is released without the 30-day isolation, and no titer test is required. GACC's own site couldn't be reached in our research (this comes from Chinese government and state-media sources), so confirm with GACC or the Chinese embassy in Japan before travel.

KR.form-ac: South Korea's APQA (Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency, apqa.go.kr — formerly QIA) publishes a Japan-specific export guide (updated August 2025), runs an online rabies antibody test application system and an export pet quarantine booking system, and issues the government certificate for Japan.
KR.gov-endorsement: In South Korea, book the export quarantine inspection through APQA's online reservation system and follow its Japan-specific guide.
KR.return-import-home: Japan is on Korea's list of rabies-free areas, so a dog coming from Japan doesn't need a rabies antibody (titer) test or a prior rabies vaccination for entry. It does need an ISO microchip and a government-issued health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service showing the microchip number and birth date. APQA quarantine officers check the documents and examine the dog on arrival. The rabies-free list can change, so confirm with APQA before travel.

PH.form-ac: In the Philippines, BAI's National Veterinary Quarantine Services Division (NVQSD) issues the Veterinary Health Certificate / International Veterinary Certificate for exporting your dog. Confirm with them how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
PH.gov-endorsement: Apply in person at BAI NVQSD (Visayas Avenue, Quezon City) or by email to nvqsd@bai.gov.ph.
PH.return-import-home: To bring your dog back you need an approved Sanitary and Phytosanitary Import Clearance (SPSIC) from BAI, applied for through the DA Trade System (about 11 working days). You'll supply vaccination and antiparasitic records, the microchip number and a photo. The dog must be at least 4 months old, and if it's getting its first rabies shot, wait 14 days before applying. From 1 January 2027 BAI will also require a rabies antibody (titer) test for SPSIC applications. Bring the health certificate from Japan's Animal Quarantine Service for inspection on arrival. Limit: 3 animals per year.

SG.form-ac: Singapore's AVS (Animal & Veterinary Service, under NParks) requires an export license (via the GoBusiness Licensing Portal) and a health certificate from a Singapore-licensed vet; AVS endorses the certificate template used alongside Japan's Form AC.
SG.gov-endorsement: In Singapore, apply for the AVS export licence through the GoBusiness Licensing Portal (S$50 standard / S$100 express). A licensed private vet issues the health certificate and AVS endorses it.
SG.return-import-home: Japan is in Singapore's Schedule II rabies category. You'll need a Singapore dog licence first, then an AVS import licence (S$50 standard / S$100 express). Your dog needs a valid rabies vaccination (inactivated or recombinant) and a rabies blood test taken at least 28 days after vaccination and at least 90 days but within 12 months before leaving Japan. A vet completes Sections I-III of the AVS health certificate, and Japan's official government veterinarian (Animal Quarantine Service) endorses Section IV. No quarantine is needed if your dog arrives within 5 days of you and has lived at the same address as you for over 6 months; otherwise there's at least 10 days of quarantine.

MY.form-ac: To export a dog from Malaysia you need an export permit from MAQIS (Malaysian Quarantine and Inspection Services) and a Veterinary Health Certificate from your DVS State office, both applied for online through the Dagangnet ePermit system. Your dog is examined at the DVS State office before the certificate is issued. Confirm with DVS how it pairs with Japan's Form AC.
MY.gov-endorsement: In Malaysia, your DVS State office examines your dog and issues the Veterinary Health Certificate; MAQIS issues the export permit (both via Dagangnet ePermit).
MY.return-import-home: Japan is one of Malaysia's 'scheduled' (rabies-free) countries. Bringing a dog back needs an import permit from MAQIS (applied for through the Dagangnet ePermit system), an ISO microchip, and a Veterinary Health Certificate from Japan's government veterinary authority confirming rabies vaccination, other core vaccines, and a recent health exam. The DVS rules for scheduled countries set no arrival quarantine. Akita and Japanese Tosa are banned breeds, and some other breeds need prior written MAQIS approval. Sabah and Sarawak have their own rules.

SE.form-ac: Sweden has no Japan-specific certificate; Jordbruksverket's generic export certificate (E9.189) is only for destinations without their own form, and Japan has one — Form AC. A Swedish official veterinarian endorses Form AC.
SE.gov-endorsement: In Sweden, an official veterinarian (officiell veterinär) endorses the certificate. Jordbruksverket (Swedish Board of Agriculture) can advise on finding one.
SE.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Sweden on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Sweden's version of the health certificate is E9.207, which you can order from Jordbruksverket before you leave; you then have 10 days to reach an EU entry point (Arlanda or Landvetter in Sweden, checked by customs). No tapeworm treatment is required.

DK.form-ac: Denmark's Fødevarestyrelsen (Danish Veterinary and Food Administration) keeps a certificate database but doesn't guarantee its contents are current. For Japan, have Fødevarestyrelsen's official vets endorse Japan's Form AC.
DK.gov-endorsement: Book an appointment with Fødevarestyrelsen's official vets (offices include Glostrup, Korsør, Herning, Vejen, Aalborg and Bornholm).
DK.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Denmark on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. The rabies vaccination must be at least 21 days old, and your dog must enter through an approved entry point. Denmark does not require tapeworm treatment.

FI.form-ac: In Finland, an official certificate is always issued by a municipal or city veterinarian (kunnaneläinlääkäri) — for Japan, they sign Japan's Form AC as the official vet. Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority) has a Japan page that refers to Japan's own requirements.
FI.gov-endorsement: Book your municipal or city veterinarian. Ruokavirasto gives advice (vienti.lemmikit@ruokavirasto.fi) and can confirm the official vet's authority afterwards if Japan asks.
FI.return-import-home: Since 22 April 2026, EU pet travel rules come from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, and Japan is on the EU's list of countries exempt from the rabies titer test, so no titer test or quarantine is needed. If your dog left Finland on its EU pet passport and its rabies vaccination is still valid when you return (no booster or blood test done in Japan), the passport is enough (EU pet passports are only for owners whose main residence is in the EU). If your dog was revaccinated or tested in Japan, it needs the new-model EU animal health certificate (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705), issued or endorsed by Japan's Animal Quarantine Service within 10 days before arrival, plus a signed owner declaration. Either way it needs its microchip. Finland also requires anti-Echinococcus tapeworm treatment 24-120 hours before arrival, documented on the certificate or passport. Customs checks your dog at Helsinki-Vantaa.

caseStudy.title: A real example: a Papillon named Miso, Canada → Japan
caseStudy.summary: One Canadian family's dog already had an ISO microchip (implanted years earlier) and one rabies vaccination. At a single vet visit he got his second rabies vaccination and the FAVN blood draw — which Japan allows, since the draw can be the same day as the second dose, as long as the first dose's immunity period hasn't run out. A dog starting from scratch can't compress it this far: the chip has to come first, then two rabies vaccinations at least 30 days apart, and only then the blood draw. Their vet also raised a couple of concerns worth knowing about in advance: whether 'blue ink' signatures were required (Japan itself doesn't specify an ink color, but CFIA confirmed in writing that it requires a wet blue-ink vet signature on the rabies vaccination certificates brought to the endorsement appointment, and recommends wet ink on the original Japan certificate — so check your own export authority's rules separately from Japan's), and which of two dates on the vaccination certificate mattered (the labeled 'due on'/next-booster date is what governs continuous coverage — a separate 'expiration' date on the same certificate turned out to be the vaccine vial's own shelf-life, not the dog's immunity window; they confirmed this in writing with their vet rather than guessing). They also learned the two deadlines fail very differently. If their trip slips past the antibody test's 2-year validity, a second blood test covers them with no new 180-day wait, as long as rabies coverage never lapses — so that only needs enough lead time for the lab result. Missing a rabies booster's labeled expiry, on the other hand, resets everything, so they keep about six weeks of buffer before each booster, on an actual calendar. Thin buffer on recoverable deadlines, fat buffer on ones that reset you to zero — that's the single biggest planning lesson from their experience.

glossary.definition: Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization test — the specific blood test Japan requires to measure your dog's rabies antibody level (titer) after vaccination. RFFIT is an accepted alternative test method.
The measured level of rabies antibodies in your dog's blood. Japan requires a result of 0.5 IU/mL or higher.
A laboratory Japan has specifically approved to run the FAVN/RFFIT test for import purposes — not every vet lab qualifies, so ask your vet which designated lab they use.
A microchip meeting the ISO 11784/11785 standard, producing a 15-digit numeric code. Japan requires this exact standard, implanted before your dog's rabies vaccination series begins.
Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries — the government body that publishes the official animal import rules and runs the Animal Quarantine Service.
Animal Quarantine Service — the Japanese government office that reviews your paperwork, both in advance (the 40-day notification) and in person at the airport on arrival.

Japan's recommended health certificate form for importing dogs and cats from non-designated regions, completed by your vet and endorsed by your government. Japan accepts another government certificate only if it contains every item Form AC covers. Designated regions use Form AB instead.

A short list of countries/regions (currently including Iceland, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Hawaii, and Guam) that Japan treats as rabies-free, allowing a simplified import process without a FAVN test. Most countries are NOT on this list.

Any country not on Japan's designated (rabies-free) list — this covers the large majority of countries, including Canada, the US mainland, the UK, and most of the EU. This is the full FAVN-based process this app focuses on.

Your country's official body that endorses export health certificates on behalf of the government — for example CFIA in Canada or APHIS in the United States. This is a separate, later step from your regular vet completing the paperwork.

faqGroups.title: Understanding your deadlines (read this one first)
faqGroups.intro: This is the part people get tripped up on. There are two clocks running at once — your FAVN blood test and your rabies vaccine's protection period — and one is forgiving while the other is not. Here's the whole thing, broken down step by step with a worked example.

items.q: How does the FAVN blood test's timing actually work?
items.a: Two numbers matter, and both are counted from the date of the blood draw: 180 days and 2 years. The 180 days is a mandatory minimum wait — your dog can't enter Japan until at least 180 days have passed since the blood was drawn (a dog that arrives early is held in quarantine at the airport for the missing days), and there's no way to speed it up. The 2 years is the shelf life of that one test result, as long as your dog's rabies vaccine coverage stays continuous the whole time (more on that below). So with a single FAVN test, your usable travel window runs from 180 days after the draw through 2 years after the draw. Example: blood drawn January 1, 2026 → you could travel any time from about June 30, 2026 through January 1, 2028, using that same test, no retesting needed in between. The 180 days counts from a passing test: if a result comes back below 0.5 IU/mL, your dog needs a new test, and the wait runs from that new, passing draw.

items.q: What if my trip might happen after that 2-year window closes?
items.a: Get a second antibody test whose result covers your arrival date. You do NOT need another 180-day wait after it, as long as three conditions all hold: your dog's rabies vaccination has been continuous since the first dose, with no lapse; the second blood draw is at least 180 days after the first one; and the second titer is 0.5 IU/mL or higher. Once those hold, the second result counts as soon as it's back from the lab, and you have 2 years from the second draw to arrive. Worked example: first FAVN drawn January 1, 2026 → valid for arrival through January 1, 2028. If your trip moves to March 2028, get a second draw any time from about June 30, 2026 onward (leaving a few weeks for lab results before you need them), and it covers you for 2 years from that new draw — even if you only draw it after the first result has expired. The 180-day gap between draws is why a retest within the first 180 days doesn't qualify for this; there's rarely a reason to retest that early unless the first result failed. Japan doesn't require you to keep retesting every 2 years — only to have a valid result for your actual arrival.

items.q: So is there a deadline for that second antibody test?
items.a: Not a strict one — that's why it's the low-stakes clock. The only real constraint is practical: the result has to be back from the lab before you need it on your paperwork, so draw it a few weeks before your pre-export vet exam. Even if your first result has already expired, MAFF accepts a new test with no fresh 180-day wait, provided the rabies vaccination never lapsed. That's very different from the rabies booster below, where being a single day late resets everything.

items.q: What's the deadline on the rabies vaccine, and why is that buffer so much bigger (a month or more)?
items.a: This is the one to genuinely watch. Your dog's rabies vaccine has a labeled protection period printed on the vaccination certificate (commonly 1 or 3 years). As long as every booster is given before the previous one's protection period runs out, coverage counts as continuous — your FAVN result stays valid for its full 2-year life, and a later retest needs no new wait. But if that coverage lapses even briefly (a booster given even a day after the old one's protection technically ran out), Japan no longer accepts your existing FAVN result at all, regardless of how much of its 2-year window was left. This is the 'reset trap': you'd have to start completely over — a new vaccination series, a brand-new FAVN blood draw, and a fresh 180-day wait — six-plus months, from zero. That's why port.dog suggests a large safety buffer here (several weeks, scaled to your vaccine's labeled duration) — enough room that a delayed vet appointment doesn't turn into a six-month setback.

items.q: So what's the simple rule for how big a buffer should be?
items.a: Size the buffer to match the cost of being late. If missing a date just costs a short, predictable delay — like getting a second antibody test back from the lab — a small buffer is plenty. If missing a date resets the whole process and costs you months — a 'hard' failure, like a lapsed rabies booster — build in a much bigger buffer, and put an actual reminder on your calendar rather than trusting yourself to remember.

items.q: Does the FAVN report need to be signed in blue ink?
items.a: Not for Japan — but your own export authority may have its own rule. Japan's official guidance does not specify a signature ink color for the FAVN report or the health certificate; it prohibits pencil, erasable pen, and correction fluid/tape, but any pen color satisfies Japan. Your country's export authority can be stricter for its own endorsement appointment. CFIA in Canada, for example, requires a wet blue-ink vet signature on the rabies vaccination certificates you bring to the endorsement appointment, and recommends a wet-ink signature on the original Japan health certificate. Ask your export authority before the appointment rather than assuming either way.

items.q: Can I use my country's generic export health certificate instead of Form AC?
items.a: Only if it contains every item Japan requires — and generic templates usually don't. Japan accepts any certificate issued or endorsed by your government that covers all the required information, but strongly recommends its own Form AC so nothing is missed. Most countries' generic 'international health certificate' templates also say not to use them when the destination supplies its own form. The exception is a country that has negotiated a Japan-specific certificate (for example the UK's EHC 6407 or Spain's ASE-3293) — that one replaces Form AC. Check your country's note on the checklist.

items.q: My dog has a heart condition (or is a flat-faced breed / senior / has mobility issues) — does that change the Japan paperwork?
items.a: Not the Japan import paperwork itself — but it absolutely matters for whether and how your dog should fly. Talk to your vet early about a fitness-to-fly assessment, and check your airline's own policies, since many restrict certain breeds or conditions from cargo or require extra documentation.

items.q: We have a brief layover or overnight stop in another country before Japan — does that need separate paperwork?
items.a: Possibly, yes. Even a same-day or overnight stop in a third country can trigger that country's own pet entry/transit rules, separate from anything Japan requires. Check directly with that country's relevant authority rather than assuming your Japan paperwork covers it.

items.q: What actually happens at the airport if something's wrong with our paperwork?
items.a: Japan's Animal Quarantine Service reviews your documents on arrival. If everything was filed correctly in advance (including the 40-day notification) and matches up, this is usually quick. If something is missing, inconsistent, or a requirement wasn't met, your dog can be held in quarantine — potentially for as long as 180 days. Getting the paperwork right in advance is worth the effort.
